---
title: "Python interpreters and editors"
---

Two Python interpreters take part in running a PHP document, and they can be
different ones.

- The kernel's interpreter is the one `juphyter install` recorded. It runs
  juphyter's Python transport and needs ipykernel 7.0 or later.
- Quarto's interpreter is the one Quarto chooses for itself when it renders.
  It needs `jupyter_client`, `nbformat`, `nbclient`, and `pyyaml`, because
  Quarto's Jupyter engine imports them before it starts any kernel. The
  environment that `juphyter install --create-venv` builds has all four,
  because it holds JupyterLab.

JupyterLab uses no third interpreter. It starts each kernel with the
interpreter that kernel's kernelspec names.

## When Quarto cannot find the kernel

When Quarto's interpreter has no Jupyter in it, Quarto can list no kernels at
all, and a render stops with:

```
ERROR: Jupyter kernel 'php' not found. Known kernels: python3
```

The PHP kernel is not the problem, and reinstalling it changes nothing. A
`jupyter: python3` document fails the same way with that interpreter. The fix
is to point Quarto at an interpreter that has Jupyter, as described below.

Two commands report the interpreter Quarto will use. `juphyter doctor` prints
it in its Quarto section. `quarto check jupyter` reports it from Quarto's side,
together with the Jupyter version and the kernels it can see:

```
Path: /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python
Jupyter: 5.9.1
Kernels: php, python3
```

A `Jupyter: (None)` line means Quarto's interpreter has no Jupyter.
`quarto check` writes to standard error, so add `2>&1` before piping it to
`grep`.

## How Quarto chooses an interpreter

Measured with Quarto 1.10.18, in order of precedence:

1. `QUARTO_PYTHON`, when the environment sets it.
2. `QUARTO_PYTHON` from a project `_environment` file. Quarto reads that file
   only when it sits beside `_quarto.yml`, and the file does not override a
   value the environment already sets.
3. The first `python3` on `PATH`.

Quarto does not read `VIRTUAL_ENV`, so an environment that is active only
through that variable is ignored. There is no fallback to `python`, and
`RETICULATE_PYTHON` has no effect.

## At a terminal

Put the environment first on `PATH` for the current shell, either with the
`export` line that `juphyter install` and `juphyter doctor` print or by
activating the environment:

```bash
source ~/.venvs/juphyter/bin/activate
quarto render notebook.qmd
```

For a single command:

```bash
QUARTO_PYTHON=~/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python quarto render notebook.qmd
```

For every render in one Quarto project, put an `_environment` file beside
`_quarto.yml`. It needs an absolute path:

```
QUARTO_PYTHON=/Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python
```

Exporting `QUARTO_PYTHON` or the environment's `PATH` entry from a shell
startup file changes the interpreter for every Quarto project on the machine,
including projects that do not use PHP. juphyter writes neither to a startup
file.

## VS Code and Cursor

Open the document's folder as a workspace. The Quarto extension asks the
Python extension for the interpreter of the workspace folder that holds the
document, and a `.qmd` opened on its own has no workspace folder to ask about.

Run **Python: Select Interpreter** from the command palette and choose an
environment that has Jupyter, such as `~/.venvs/juphyter`. The Quarto extension
passes that choice to Quarto as `QUARTO_PYTHON` on every render in the
workspace. Nothing outside the workspace changes.

Because the extension sets `QUARTO_PYTHON`, a project `_environment` file
cannot override the selection. A wrong selection is corrected in the
interpreter picker.

## Positron

Positron bundles the same Python extension and the same Quarto extension, so
the steps are the same: open the folder, then run **Python: Select
Interpreter**.

A workspace that already has an interpreter stored keeps it.
`python.defaultInterpreterPath` in `.vscode/settings.json` applies only when no
interpreter has been selected, so a stored choice is replaced through the
picker. A change to that setting takes effect after **Developer: Reload
Window**.

Positron opens a new terminal for each render, so the interpreter it passed to
Quarto can be read there:

```bash
echo "QUARTO_PYTHON=[$QUARTO_PYTHON]"
```

An empty value means no interpreter is selected for the workspace.

## Other editors

An editor without Quarto integration, such as PhpStorm, leaves the choice to
`PATH`. Activate the environment before starting the editor, or set
`QUARTO_PYTHON` in its terminal or run configuration.

RStudio is in this group. It sets no `QUARTO_PYTHON` of its own, and Quarto
does not read the Python preference that RStudio stores.

## When no Python can host the kernel

`juphyter install` looks for an interpreter in this order: the one named by
`--python`, then the one that owns the `jupyter` command on `PATH`, read from
that script's first line. When the interpreter it found has no ipykernel 7, it
builds a virtual environment with JupyterLab instead of installing into the
existing interpreter.

System and Homebrew Python builds are marked as externally managed, and
`pip install` into them refuses. A virtual environment avoids that.

- `--create-venv PATH` names where to build it.
- Without `--create-venv`, the command asks before building one at
  `~/.venvs/juphyter`, and builds it without asking when there is no terminal.
- An environment that already exists at that path is reused, and its packages
  are installed again, so a second run finishes an interrupted one.
- A directory that exists and holds something other than an environment is
  refused.
- With `--python`, the command builds nothing. When the named interpreter has
  no ipykernel, it prints the `pip install` command for that interpreter and
  writes no kernel.
